source.title: Resisted Sled Sprint Training to Improve Sprint Performance: A Systematic Review

paper.citation: Petrakos G., Morin J.B., Egan B. Resisted Sled Sprint Training to Improve Sprint Performance: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2016;46(3):381-400. doi:10.1007/s40279-015-0422-8.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How effective is resisted sled sprint training compared with unresisted sprint training, and how do sled loads influence acceleration and maximal-velocity outcomes? Participants: Athletes from 11 eligible longitudinal training studies. Sport and level: Sprint-trained, strength-trained, and team-sport participants. Design: Systematic review. Exposure or intervention: Resisted sled sprint training prescribed by percentage body mass, velocity decrement, or absolute load.
paper.tldr: Eleven studies met the eligibility criteria, with load prescribed inconsistently as body-mass percentage, velocity decrement, or absolute kilograms. Light loading below 10% body mass or 10% velocity decrement ranged from a 1.5% decrement in acceleration (effect size 0.50) to a 2.4% improvement in maximal velocity (effect size 0.80) in sprint-trained participants. Program sled work from the target adaptation rather than a universal percent-body-mass rule.
paper.methods: Design: Systematic review. Exposure or intervention: Resisted sled sprint training prescribed by percentage body mass, velocity decrement, or absolute load. Comparator: Unresisted sprint training and different sled-load categories. Measurements and outcomes: Acceleration and maximal sprint velocity, summarized with percentage changes and Cohen's d. Analysis: PubMed and SPORTDiscus search with eligibility filtering and effect-size comparison.
paper.findings: Eleven studies met the eligibility criteria, with load prescribed inconsistently as body-mass percentage, velocity decrement, or absolute kilograms. Light loading below 10% body mass or 10% velocity decrement ranged from a 1.5% decrement in acceleration (effect size 0.50) to a 2.4% improvement in maximal velocity (effect size 0.80) in sprint-trained participants. Loads from moderate to very heavy produced acceleration changes from 0.5% to 9.1% with effect sizes from 0.14 to 4.00, but superiority over unresisted sprinting remained equivocal.
paper.limitations: Between-study comparison was limited by differences in participant training status, training phase, and load prescription. The review could not define an optimal sled load or volume for each sprint outcome.
paper.practicalImplications: Program sled work from the target adaptation rather than a universal percent-body-mass rule. Record velocity decrement so the actual resistance stimulus is visible, retain unresisted sprint exposure, and monitor whether the intended part of the sprint improves. The evidence supports sleds as a potentially useful option, not an automatically superior one.
